headline: Highest risk is medium prompt-injection and cascading-error from ctx’s filesystem/MCP hooks feeding langchain4j workflows; no direct evidence of shared channels or sensitive-data egress.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ctx explicitly observes Claude Code PostToolUse/Stop events and touches filesystem/MCP surfaces, so its outputs can be fed into downstream parsing. langchain4j is a framework that can consume model outputs in support workflows; the pairwise bridge is inferred, not directly documented, so uncertainty pushes above low.
conditions: IF ctx event output is copied into langchain4j prompts or parsers without provenance checks
IF either side treats file or hook content as trusted instructions
mitigations: Add a provenance prefix to ctx hook output before passing it onward
Disable automatic instruction-following on any imported text
Review one sample end-to-end message path for prompt markers
Use a separate workspace for ctx-generated artifacts
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and allowlist parsing

B_data_leakage.rationale: ctx touches audit/runtime logs, graph data, and filesystem, but langchain4j’s profile shows no data classes touched and network egress is none. With no shared workspace or upload path documented, leakage is possible only through unusual operator wiring, so the blast radius appears small and indirect.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same local workspace
IF ctx logs or graph data are manually forwarded into langchain4j inputs
mitigations: Keep separate directories for each agent
Rotate or redact logs before handoff
Verify langchain4j runs with network egress disabled
Limit ctx to non-sensitive test data
requires-engineering: enforce workspace isolation at the orchestrator

C_capability_conflict.rationale: ctx can install packages and write to filesystem, while langchain4j is a framework that may also manipulate files or shared resources when embedded. No locking or shared-resource coordination is documented, so overlapping writes are plausible in default integration patterns, though not proven high because langchain4j’s direct write surface is not explicit.
conditions: IF both agents are configured to modify the same directory or build state
IF the orchestrator does not serialize package or file writes
mitigations: Assign distinct working directories
Avoid concurrent package installation
Run one agent at a time for shared resources
Check for lockfiles before writes
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level mutexes

D_cascading_error.rationale: ctx can emit hook-derived context and logs, and langchain4j can consume model outputs in application flows. If langchain4j treats ctx output as authoritative, errors can cascade into downstream support actions or generated responses. The interaction is inferred from profiles rather than directly observed, so medium is safer than low.
conditions: IF langchain4j uses ctx output as a source of truth without verification
IF downstream actions are triggered from those outputs
mitigations: Insert a human review step before acting on ctx output
Require citations or source IDs in forwarded content
Compare ctx output against an independent source
Log and sample-check one full workflow run
requires-engineering: add validation gates before action execution

E_compliance.rationale: ctx touches audit/runtime logs and graph data, which can create retention or residency concerns, but langchain4j’s profile does not specify regulated data handling or residency constraints. With only one side showing compliance-relevant data classes and no documented mismatch, this is a low, localized risk rather than a breach pathway.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in ctx logs or graph data
IF those artifacts are retained or exported through a separate policy
mitigations: Classify the data before use
Exclude regulated records from ctx runs
Set a short log-retention window
Review residency settings for any storage backend
requires-engineering: document and enforce retention policy
